documents.title: Academic Integrity Policy (file name 2011-03; includes AI language)
documents.summary: Seattle University's registrar-hosted Academic Integrity Policy is an all-purpose integrity policy that names generative AI in its plagiarism definition and a cheating example, leaves AI prohibitions to faculty, and sets the reporting, appeal and sanction process used for AI cases. It does not give students a list of allowed uses.
documents.stance_why: The policy says 'Faculty members are permitted to have specific policies regarding the use of AI programs, including prohibiting their use' and treats AI output as cheating only 'if prohibited by the faculty member', so it sets no university-wide ban or permission and hands the decision to instructors, apart from requiring citation of AI output.

units.why: The definition names 'the outputs of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) programs' presented as one's own without citation as plagiarism, so uncited AI output becomes an integrity offense; classed P36 (misconduct) rather than P24 because it defines the violation, with the citation duty in the next unit.
units.anchor: outputs of Generative Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) programs when presented as one’s own work
units.frag_start: The use of the work or
units.fit_note: Also says intent is irrelevant: undisclosed AI output is plagiarism 'regardless of intent'.

units.why: Examples of plagiarism include code or papers from 'AI program’s output without proper citation and/or acknowledgment, as required by faculty', so students must cite or acknowledge AI output where faculty require it; P24 fits because the rule is about citation/acknowledgment.
units.anchor: person’s work or AI program’s output without proper citation and/or acknowledgment, as required by faculty
units.fit_note: Citation duty is conditional on faculty requirement and explicitly covers code.

units.why: The cheating list includes 'Using AI output for any form of academic work' for writing, programming or mathematics 'if prohibited by the faculty member', so AI use becomes cheating only when the instructor bans it; chosen P36 (classification as misconduct) rather than P04 because the sentence defines a violation.
units.anchor: mathematics assignments if prohibited by the faculty member
units.frag_start: Using AI output for any form
units.frag_end: if prohibited by the faculty member.
units.policy: Using AI output for academic work, including writing, programming, computer programming or mathematics assignments, is cheating if the faculty member prohibits it.
units.fit_note: The misconduct classification depends on a faculty prohibition; it names programming and mathematics explicitly.

units.why: The note says 'Faculty members are permitted to have specific policies regarding the use of AI programs, including prohibiting their use', handing the stance to instructors; P04 fits because the decision is left per instructor.
units.anchor: Faculty members are permitted to have specific policies regarding the use of AI programs

units.why: The same note says such policies 'should be communicated to students at the beginning of the course or at the time when a task or assignment is officially given', which is a duty to communicate expectations; P09 covers stating expectations in the syllabus or assignment.
units.anchor: such policies should be communicated to students at the beginning of the course
units.fit_note: Allows communication at course start or when the assignment is given, not only in the syllabus.

units.why: The devices rule says 'The use of any electronic device during an examination is expressly prohibited unless explicitly authorized by the instructor', which is a closed-device exam rule and so covers AI-capable devices; P22 fits though it names devices, not AI.
units.anchor: use of any electronic device during an examination is expressly prohibited unless explicitly authorized
units.fit_note: Does not mention AI; it is a general closed-device rule that bears on AI during exams.

units.why: Students are told they 'are responsible for educating themselves as to the proper mode of attributing credit in any course or field', which applies to AI output because the plagiarism definition covers it; P78 fits (students learn each course's rules).
units.anchor: Students are responsible for educating themselves as to the proper mode of attributing credit
units.fit_note: Not AI-specific; it covers attribution rules generally, including those for AI output.

units.why: Faculty 'may decide, if appropriate, to first investigate a potential academic integrity violation' and then notify the student, which sets the first procedural step for suspected misuse including AI; P81 fits as formal reporting procedure.

units.why: The notice must include 'a description of the violation and any evidence or rationale that supports the allegation', giving the student the basis of the allegation; P64 (fairness and right to respond) fits better than P69 because it concerns what the student is told, not the standard of proof.
units.anchor: include a description of the violation and any evidence or rationale that supports the allegation

units.why: The policy says the faculty member 'should schedule a meeting to discuss the alleged academic integrity violation with the student', so the instructor speaks with the student before sanctioning; P57 fits.

documents.title: Guidelines for AI Use in Teaching and Research
documents.summary: A faculty-focused guideline from the Technology Ethics Initiative, adopted by the Academic Technology Committee, setting out principles for AI in teaching (educational benefit, academic integrity, data privacy) and in research. It declines a blanket rule and tells instructors to set course-specific policies, state them in syllabi, ask for acknowledgment of AI use, and not rely on detectors.
documents.stance_why: The text says 'an outright permission or ban is a poor substitute for instructor leadership' and urges 'every faculty member' to 'establish course-specific policies', so it sets no university-wide stance and delegates the decision to instructors.

units.why: The guidelines were 'drafted, deliberated on, and adopted by the Academic Technology Committee, which operates under Academic Assembly', stating how the guidance was made; P84 fits.
units.anchor: drafted, deliberated on, and adopted by the Academic Technology Committee

units.why: The university 'values the coherent and effective adoption of technology, AI included, in every field and level of higher education', a welcoming default toward AI; P02 fits though it is expressed as a value, not a rule.
units.anchor: values the coherent and effective adoption of technology, AI included, in every field
units.fit_note: A statement of institutional value, not a rule binding students.

units.why: Departments are 'encouraged to explore uses of AI appropriate to their fields of study' and to 'conduct in-depth analyses', leaving field-specific rules to units; P85 fits.
units.anchor: Academic departments and programs are encouraged to explore uses of AI appropriate to their fields

units.why: The goal is stated as making sure AI use 'provides educational benefits, respects the rules of academic integrity and avoids privacy violations or data leaks', which sets purpose and principles; P56 fits.
units.anchor: use of AI provides educational benefits, respects the rules of academic integrity
units.frag_start: Educators' goal is to make sure

units.why: The guidelines say the university 'should provide guidance, training and support through the Technology Ethics Initiative, the Center for Faculty Development', a promise of faculty and community support; P63 fits.
units.anchor: Seattle University should provide guidance, training and support through the Technology Ethics Initiative

units.why: 'An outright permission or ban is a poor substitute for instructor leadership' says the university sets neither a blanket ban nor permission; P04 fits because the decision rests with instructors.
units.anchor: an outright permission or ban is a poor substitute for instructor leadership

units.why: The text says educational value 'depends on factors like the subject, students' learning needs, instructors' pedagogical approaches and preferences, and course and assessment design', so allowed use depends on course context; P83 is the nearest type (follow from course aims), though it names more factors than objectives.
units.anchor: depends on factors like the subject, students' learning needs, instructors' pedagogical approaches
units.fit_note: Lists several context factors (subject, learner needs, pedagogy, assessment), not only learning objectives.

units.why: 'Every program and department is encouraged to prepare guidelines for effective and discipline-specific AI use' invites units to write their own rules; P85 fits.
units.anchor: Every program and department is encouraged to prepare guidelines for effective and discipline-specific AI use

units.why: Faculty and administrators 'should ideally adopt AI tools that eliminate hallucinations', a criterion for choosing tools; P65 is the nearest type (review and approve AI tools) although it states a quality criterion, not a review process.
units.anchor: Faculty and administrators should ideally adopt AI tools that
units.fit_note: Sets accuracy as a criterion for adopting tools, with no approval process.

units.why: 'Faculty should instruct students about the possibility of hallucinations, preferably in course syllabi, so that the students know to verify AI-generated information', which tells instructors to teach verification; P31 fits.
units.anchor: Faculty should instruct students about the possibility of hallucinations, preferably in

units.anchor: AI may threaten the process of learning, as commercial AI tools can generate content

notes: No computing, school or course documents were collected for Seattle University; coded only the three included university-layer documents. The syllabus template's AI section is optional guidance (not marked required). Repeated sample text in samples 2 and 3 is coded once. Appeal and sanction units in the academic integrity policy apply to AI cases as general integrity process, not AI-specific text.
